disclaimer: This report is for educational and wellness purposes only. It is not a medical diagnosis and does not replace advice from a qualified healthcare professional. HbA1c results should be confirmed by your doctor. Do not start, stop or change any medication without medical advice.

status.label: In the prediabetes range
status.explanation: Your HbA1c is between 5.7% and 6.4%, the range used for prediabetes. This is a common and often reversible stage where lifestyle changes make the biggest difference.

summary: Your HbA1c is in the prediabetes range, which means this is a good time to make changes that can help keep your blood sugar from rising further. Your BMI is in the obese range, and combined with low physical activity, regular alcohol use, and your age, this raises your overall risk. Your sleep apnoea and obesity can also make blood sugar harder to manage. The most valuable next steps are getting your HbA1c and liver health checked as highlighted, working toward gradual weight loss, and building more regular movement into your day.

comorbidity_assessment.note: Poor sleep quality from untreated sleep apnoea can raise stress hormones and make blood sugar harder to control, so staying consistent with any breathing device and sleep schedule matters.
Extra body weight, especially around the middle, can make the body less responsive to insulin, so gradual weight loss can help improve blood sugar levels over time.

constraints: Avoid alcohol and heavy meals within 3 hours of bedtime.
Follow the calorie target; avoid sugary drinks and fruit juices completely.
Fill half the plate with non-starchy vegetables to stay full on fewer calories.

foods_to_eat: Non-starchy vegetables like zucchini, spinach, peppers and tomatoes
Whole grains such as bulgur, farro and whole oats
Fatty fish such as salmon and sardines
Olive oil as the main fat source
Nuts and seeds in small portions
foods_to_avoid: Deep-fried foods like fried calamari or chips
Sweets, baklava and other sugary desserts
Processed meats like sausages and salami
Excess cheese and high-fat cream sauces
plan.portion_guidance: Fill half your plate with non-starchy vegetables, one quarter with lean protein like fish, chicken or legumes, and one quarter with whole grains like bulgur or whole oats. Use household measures such as a palm-sized portion for protein and a cupped hand for grains to help manage portions without needing to weigh food.
plan.hydration: Aim for 8 to 10 glasses of water through the day. Herbal tea and plain sparkling water are good options. Avoid sugary drinks, fruit juices and limit alcohol, especially within 3 hours of bedtime.
based_on: obesity and sleep apnoea: smaller, vegetable-filled meals
avoid alcohol and heavy meals before bedtime
regular alcohol use: guidance to limit and avoid near bedtime

exercise: Since you're currently sedentary, start with 10–15 minutes of gentle activity, like walking or stationary cycling, 3–4 times a week.
Gradually build up over several weeks toward the goal of 150 minutes a week of moderate activity, going slowly to protect your joints given your weight.
Add simple muscle-strengthening exercises (like bodyweight squats, resistance bands, or light weights) on 2 non-consecutive days a week.
Choose low-impact options first, such as swimming or using an elliptical machine, to reduce strain on your joints.
lifestyle.walking_goal: Start with a 10-minute walk after one meal each day, 5 days a week. Over the next 4-6 weeks, work up to 30 minutes a day, 5 days a week, at a pace that feels moderately brisk.
lifestyle.weight_management: Your BMI is in the obese range, and gradual weight loss can meaningfully help reduce the severity of your sleep apnoea and improve your HbA1c trend. Aim for a steady, sustainable loss of about 5-10% of your current body weight over the next 6 months, which works out to small, manageable weekly changes rather than a fast transformation. Focus on consistent habits—regular meals, more activity, and good sleep—rather than quick fixes.
lifestyle.sleep: Try to get 7-9 hours of sleep each night on a consistent schedule, going to bed and waking up at the same times even on weekends. Since you have sleep apnoea, it's especially important to use any prescribed breathing device (such as CPAP) every night, including during naps, to get the full benefit. Keep your bedroom cool, dark, and quiet, and avoid screens for 30-60 minutes before bed.
stress: Try a daily 5-10 minute breathing exercise, such as slow belly breathing, to help calm your nervous system.
Consider a short daily mindfulness or meditation practice using a free app or guided audio.
Regular physical activity, like your daily walks, can also help lower stress over time.
Make time for a hobby or social connection each week, since relaxation and enjoyment support long-term stress management.
behaviour_change: Since you drink regularly, consider cutting down gradually; try setting alcohol-free days each week and tracking how much you drink to notice patterns.
As a former smoker, staying smoke-free is a great achievement for your heart and lung health; if you ever feel at risk of returning to smoking, quitlines and your doctor can offer support.
Build small, consistent habits, like a daily walk and a fixed bedtime, since steady routines are more sustainable than big sudden changes.
Track your progress (sleep, activity, weight) weekly to notice trends and stay motivated, celebrating small wins along the way.

monitoring.name: HbA1c
monitoring.why: Catches progression from prediabetes to diabetes early.

monitoring.name: Liver check (liver tests and FIB-4 score)
monitoring.why: Fatty liver is common with diabetes and obesity and can progress without symptoms.
monitoring.frequency: FIB-4 score every 1–2 years, or sooner if your doctor finds a higher risk

monitoring.name: Fasting blood sugar
monitoring.why: Shows your blood glucose after an overnight fast and complements HbA1c.
monitoring.frequency: Alongside your HbA1c test, or as your doctor advises

monitoring.name: Vitamin D
monitoring.why: Low vitamin D is more common with obesity and kidney disease; testing is not routine for everyone.
monitoring.frequency: Only if your doctor recommends it

monitoring.name: Blood pressure
monitoring.why: High blood pressure multiplies the heart and kidney risks of high blood glucose.
monitoring.frequency: At every doctor visit; at home regularly if you have high blood pressure

preventive_actions: Follow your calorie target of 1850 calories and fill half your plate with non-starchy vegetables.
Avoid alcohol and heavy meals within three hours of bedtime to support better sleep and glucose levels.
Start physical activity gently, building up slowly to protect your joints while increasing movement over time.
Keep a consistent sleep schedule and use any prescribed breathing device every night.
Schedule your highlighted HbA1c and liver checks as recommended.
Aim for a realistic, gradual weight loss goal of 5-10% of your body weight over six months.

hba1c_caveat: HbA1c can be less accurate if you have anaemia, kidney disease, a recent blood transfusion or certain haemoglobin variants.
